This **Pilot Protoplanetary Disk Catalog** is an educational and scientific resource designed to explore the physical properties, morphologies, and evolutionary processes of **protoplanetary disks**.

This pilot version combines short scientific summaries, representative images, comparative tables, and introductory programming activities based on real astronomical data products.

## Activities {#activities}

This catalog includes a **FITS-based data science activity** designed to help students explore real astronomical data and analyze how disk substructures can be measured from images.

Este catálogo incluye una **actividad de ciencia de datos basada en imágenes FITS** pensada para que los estudiantes trabajen con datos astronómicos reales y analicen cómo se pueden medir subestructuras de discos a partir de imágenes.

::: {.activity-grid}

::: {.activity-card}
### Activity / English version

**Morphological analysis of radial substructures**

Use a real FITS image of **IM Lup** or **HD 163296** to deproject the disk, transform the image into polar coordinates, build a radial intensity profile, and identify rings, gaps, or radial depressions.

[Open English version →](activity_morphology_en.html){.disk-link}
:::

::: {.activity-card}
### Actividad / Versión en español

**Análisis morfológico de subestructuras radiales**

Usa una imagen FITS real de **IM Lup** o **HD 163296** para deproyectar el disco, transformarlo a coordenadas polares, construir un perfil radial de intensidad e identificar anillos, brechas o depresiones radiales.

[Abrir versión en español →](activity_morphology_es.html){.disk-link}
:::


:::

## What is a protoplanetary disk?

A protoplanetary disk is a young, flattened structure that forms around a star during its earliest stages, when part of the collapsing material no longer falls directly onto the protostar but instead settles into orbit through “angular momentum conservation” [@williams2011; @andrews2020]. In this sense, it can be understood as a “flattened disk of gas and solids” that accompanies the young star and gathers the material from which the system will continue to evolve. These disks are also the “material reservoirs and birthplaces of planetary systems,” because they host the processes that may eventually lead to the formation of planets [@andrews2020].

Their connection to young stars is therefore direct: they appear “shortly after their birth” and are studied especially around visible young stars such as **T Tauri stars**, during early phases like **Class II YSOs** [@williams2011]. In general, they “form almost immediately after a molecular core collapses,” and they show “an inherent and large diversity in initial disk sizes and masses” [@williams2011]. Once the initial envelope has dispersed, the system is already “truly protoplanetary, not protostellar”; at that stage, the disk contains only “a few percent of the central stellar mass,” usually has a “flared” geometry, and shows approximately “Keplerian” motions, features that describe its basic shape and dynamics [@williams2011].

These disks not only store material, but also provide the setting where planet formation begins. In the “core accretion model,” dust grains grow through several stages until they become rocks, planetesimals, and protoplanetary cores capable of capturing gas [@williams2011]. For that reason, studying the mass, structure, and evolution of a disk helps us understand not only how a young system changes over time, but also what kinds of planets may form within it and how their properties depend on the disk’s physical conditions [@andrews2020].

### How do we observe protoplanetary disks?

Protoplanetary disks are studied at different wavelengths because each tracer reveals a different part of their structure [@andrews2020]. In the optical and near-infrared, “scattered light” primarily traces small dust grains in the disk surface; in the mid-infrared, warmer dust in the inner regions is more easily detected; and at sub-mm/mm wavelengths, “thermal continuum emission” is used to study the distribution of colder solids, while “spectral line emission” probes the properties and dynamics of the gas [@andrews2020]. Because many disks are cold, small on the sky, and emit efficiently at millimeter wavelengths, “radio interferometry” has become essential, and much of the recent progress in the field has been driven by **ALMA**, one of the most important tools for studying protoplanetary disks and their substructures [@andrews2020].

---

::: {.substructure-grid-clean}

::: {.substructure-row}
::: {.substructure-name}
Ring
:::
::: {.substructure-text}
A bright band in the disk, where the emission increases compared with the neighboring regions. In images, it appears as a relatively narrow annulus that stands out from the surrounding material.
:::
:::

::: {.substructure-row}
::: {.substructure-name}
Gap
:::
::: {.substructure-text}
A dimmer band between brighter rings. In millimeter continuum observations, it is usually interpreted as a local reduction of millimeter-sized dust relative to the adjacent rings, not as a completely empty region.
:::
:::

::: {.substructure-row}
::: {.substructure-name}
Cavity
:::
::: {.substructure-text}
A large inner region with much weaker emission, usually surrounded by a bright outer ring. Unlike a gap, which is a narrow depression between rings, a cavity is a broader central clearing in the disk structure.
:::
:::

::: {.substructure-row}
::: {.substructure-name}
Arc
:::
::: {.substructure-text}
A bright feature that covers only part of the disk instead of forming a full circle. It can appear as a partial ring or as a localized concentration of emission in one sector of the disk.
:::
:::

::: {.substructure-row}
::: {.substructure-name}
Spiral
:::
::: {.substructure-text}
A curved arm-like feature that extends through the disk. These structures can look more open or more tightly wrapped depending on the system.
:::
:::

:::

## Dust and gas do not trace the same disk

A protoplanetary disk does not look the same in every tracer because each observation highlights a different physical component of the system. As Andrews explains, “the first two are sensitive to the physical conditions and distribution of the solids, and the third is used to measure the properties of the gas” [@andrews2020]. In the dust component, this difference depends not only on the instrument but also on how particles evolve within the disk: Birnstiel notes that “starlight scattered by small dust in the disk surface as well as the thermal continuum emission of the dust particles themselves are the most readily available observational tracers,” but they do not probe the same grain population [@birnstiel2024_dustgrowth]. Small grains remain better mixed in the disk surface, whereas larger grains tend to settle toward the midplane, drift radially, and concentrate at pressure maxima. Aikawa, Okuzumi, and Pontoppidan add that ALMA has revealed “grain growth, gas-dust decoupling, and sub-structures such as rings and gaps in the dust continuum,” while “molecular line observations” provide constraints on the radial and vertical structure of molecular abundances as well as on gas dynamics such as turbulence [@aikawa2024]. For that reason, the same disk can look significantly different in scattered light, thermal continuum emission, and molecular lines, and that is precisely why this catalog separates the sections **Dust in the disk** and **Gas in the disk**.

A useful example is **HD 100546**. Pérez et al. (2020) used long-baseline ALMA observations to compare the 1.3 mm dust continuum with molecular-line emission from CO isotopologues. In the continuum, the disk shows a wide dust ring with fine radial and azimuthal structure, described by the authors as a “complex maze of ridges and trenches”. However, the gas does not simply reproduce the same pattern: the ^12^CO channel maps show “wiggles or kinks that deviate from Keplerian kinematics”, especially near the continuum ring. The same kinematic signature is weaker or absent in the rarer isotopologues ^13^CO and C^18^O, suggesting that the perturbation changes with disk height. This makes HD 100546 a clear example of why dust images and gas kinematics must be read together: the dust reveals where solid material is concentrated, while the gas reveals motions, vertical structure, and possible dynamical perturbations associated with planet–disk interactions [@perez2020_hd100546].

## From dust to planets

::: {.dust-planets-section}

::: {.dust-intro-box}
The path from dust to planets begins with extremely small particles. In protoplanetary disks, the solid material starts at sizes of “≲ 1 µm” [@birnstiel2024_dustgrowth]. From there, grains collide, settle, drift, and sometimes become trapped in pressure structures. These processes make planet formation possible, but also difficult: solids must grow while avoiding destructive collisions and rapid inward drift.
:::

::: {.dust-pathway-grid}

::: {.dust-pathway-card}
### 1. Growth and settling

Grains collide, and when those collisions are gentle enough, they can stick together and form progressively larger aggregates. As Williams & Cieza explain, “grain growth and dust settling are intimately interconnected processes,” because as grains grow, they become less coupled to the gas and begin to settle toward the disk midplane, although turbulence can still stir some material upward [@williams2011].
:::

::: {.dust-pathway-card}
### 2. Radial drift and barriers

As dust grows, its aerodynamic interaction with the gas becomes increasingly important. Birnstiel notes that particles experience a “drag force” when they move relative to the gas, while the gas orbits in a “slightly sub-Keplerian” way [@birnstiel2024_dustgrowth]. This creates a headwind that removes angular momentum from solids and causes **radial drift**. Growth can also become “growth-neutral or even destructive,” so aggregates may bounce, fragment, or erode instead of continuing to grow [@birnstiel2024_dustgrowth].
:::

::: {.dust-pathway-card}
### 3. Dust traps and planetesimals

Regions where dust no longer drifts inward so efficiently are especially important. When particles encounter a local pressure maximum, Birnstiel explains that “dust can be trapped,” allowing solids to accumulate into dense concentrations [@birnstiel2024_dustgrowth]. These concentrations can create conditions in which “planetesimal formation becomes possible” [@birnstiel2024_dustgrowth].
:::

:::

::: {.dust-bridge-box}
In this sense, **dust traps** link the physical evolution of solids with the appearance of rings, gaps, and other substructures. They also provide a bridge between observable disk morphology and the formation of planetesimals, which can later become the building blocks of planetary cores.
:::

::: {.planet-example-grid}

::: {.planet-example-card}
::: {.example-label}
Low-mass planet formation
:::

### HD 169142: a possible mini-Neptune

A concrete example of this connection between dust and planet formation is the disk of **HD 169142**. Pérez et al. (2019) used high-resolution ALMA observations at 1.3 mm to resolve the outer disk into three narrow rings, showing that an apparently complex dust architecture can be related to the presence of a low-mass planet. The study emphasizes that the formation of pebbles, planetesimals, and planetary cores relies on “radial pressure bumps,” where the inward drift of solids can slow down and dust can accumulate.

For HD 169142, the authors propose that the outer rings can be explained by “a single migrating low mass planet (10 M⊕)”. This planet, comparable to a mini-Neptune, would migrate inward and reshape the dust distribution, producing narrow rings and gaps around its orbit. This makes HD 169142 a useful example of how dust is not only the raw material for building planets, but also an observational tracer of protoplanets that may not be directly detected yet. In this case, the interpretation favors a gradual formation pathway, or “bottom-up process such as core accretion”, capable of producing a planetary embryo in the outer region of the disk [@perez2019_mini_neptune].
:::

::: {.planet-example-card}
::: {.example-label}
Giant planets and circumplanetary material
:::

### V4046 Sgr: dust traps and a possible CPD shadow

A complementary example is the circumbinary disk of **V4046 Sgr**, where dust structures may trace a more advanced planetary architecture. Weber et al. (2022) combined hydrodynamical simulations and radiative transfer calculations to compare models with near-infrared scattered-light and millimeter observations. Their model suggests that the observed rings and gaps are consistent with two giant planets, located at approximately 9 au and 20 au, with a pressure maximum between them where dust can accumulate.

This case extends the idea of dust traps toward giant planet formation and circumplanetary material. The authors describe the ring structure as “diffusion-balanced dust trapping within the gas pressure maxima”, meaning that dust concentration is shaped by the balance between confinement toward a pressure maximum and diffusion. The study also proposes that a localized decrease in scattered-light brightness may be explained as a “shadow cast by a circumplanetary disc”. In this way, V4046 Sgr illustrates that dust substructures can not only trace embedded planets, but may also reveal circumplanetary material associated with them [@weber2022_v4046sgr].
:::

:::

:::

## After the protoplanetary phase

::: {.after-phase-section}

::: {.after-phase-hero}
::: {.after-phase-kicker}
Evolutionary context
:::

This catalog focuses on protoplanetary disks, but the evolution of a planetary system does not end when the primordial disk begins to disperse. At later stages, systems may host **debris disks**, where the dust is no longer mainly the original material of the young disk, but is instead continually replenished by collisions between larger bodies such as planetesimals, asteroids, or comet-like objects.
:::

::: {.debris-showcase}

::: {.debris-figure-card}
![](images/disco_escombros.jpg){.debris-image}

::: {.debris-caption}
*ALMA image of the debris ring around Fomalhaut, a nearby bright star located about 25 light-years away. The ring is made of dusty debris released by collisions among exocomets and small bodies, illustrating a later evolutionary stage than the gas-rich protoplanetary disks presented in this catalog.*

**Credit:** ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO) / L. Matrà / M. A. MacGregor
:::
:::

::: {.debris-definition-card}
### What is a debris disk?

::: {.debris-point}
**Gas content:** debris disks were traditionally considered almost gas-poor systems, or “gas-free environments”, because the primordial gas from the protoplanetary disk was expected to have disappeared.
:::

::: {.debris-point}
**Dust origin:** unlike protoplanetary disks, the dust in debris disks is usually second-generation material, replenished by collisions.
:::

::: {.debris-point}
**Evolutionary role:** debris disks help us understand what can remain after the main planet-forming phase.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.hybrid-study-card}
### HD 121617: a possible hybrid disk

Recent observations show that some debris disks still contain gas. A useful example is **HD 121617**, studied by Weber et al. (2026) as part of the ARKS survey. In this system, ALMA observes a narrow ring with a bright arc in millimeter emission, while VLT/SPHERE shows a more symmetric scattered-light ring that is shifted slightly outward.

::: {.hybrid-mini-grid}

::: {.hybrid-mini-card}
#### What do the observations suggest?

The study proposes that the observed structure may be explained by **dust–gas interactions**. In this scenario, an unstable gas ring can create a radial and azimuthal dust trap: millimeter-sized grains concentrate in the arc seen by ALMA, while smaller grains, more affected by stellar radiation pressure, appear farther out in scattered light.
:::

::: {.hybrid-mini-card}
#### Why is this important?

If the ALMA asymmetry is caused by gas drag, then HD 121617 would require more total gas than what is inferred from CO alone. This could imply the presence of primordial gas left over from the protoplanetary disk phase. For that reason, the authors suggest that HD 121617 may be a **“hybrid disc”**, a system “bridging the protoplanetary and debris disc stages” [@weber2026_arks_ix].
:::

:::

::: {.after-phase-takeaway}
**Key idea:** debris disks are not simply the “end” of disk evolution. Some may still preserve gas and show dust–gas interactions, making them valuable systems for connecting protoplanetary disks with later planetary-system stages.
:::

:::

:::

## How do protoplanetary disks evolve and develop substructures?

::: {.disk-evolution-section}

::: {.evolution-intro-box}
The evolution of a protoplanetary disk can be understood as a process of **redistributing material and angular momentum**. Because these disks form through “angular momentum conservation,” gas cannot fall directly onto the star; in order to accrete, it must transfer part of its orbital motion to other regions of the disk [@williams2011]. For that reason, while some material gradually moves inward, another part can spread outward; in this sense, the disk can “accrete onto the star while simultaneously spreading diffusively to large radii” [@armitage2011].
:::

::: {.evolution-mechanism-grid}

::: {.evolution-mechanism-card}
### Angular momentum transport

Disk evolution is often described through an **effective viscosity**, understood not as ordinary molecular friction but as a simplified way to represent angular momentum transport. In many models, that efficiency is summarized with the **α parameter** [@armitage2011].
:::

::: {.evolution-mechanism-card}
### Turbulence and self-gravity

Among the relevant mechanisms are the **MRI**, which can “initiate and sustain MHD turbulence,” and **self-gravity**, which in sufficiently cold and massive disks can generate “trailing spiral arms” and redistribute both mass and angular momentum [@armitage2011].
:::

::: {.evolution-mechanism-card}
### Pressure maxima and substructures

Many observed substructures likely trace **local gas pressure maxima**, where the migration of solids slows down and material can accumulate. These pressure maxima may arise from **fluid instabilities** or **planet–disk interactions**, producing rings, gaps, spirals, asymmetries, arcs, or crescent-like features [@andrews2020].
:::

:::

::: {.evolution-example-grid}

::: {.evolution-example-card}
::: {.example-label}
Gravitational instability
:::

### Elias 2-27: spiral arms in a massive disk

An example of this diversity is **Elias 2-27**, a disk with two prominent spiral arms observed in the millimeter dust continuum. Paneque-Carreño et al. (2021) analyzed ALMA observations at several wavelengths and found that the spiral morphology is recovered in the dust emission, while the gas also shows strong kinematic perturbations associated with the spiral regions.

In this system, the spirals are interpreted as possible evidence of gravitational instability: a process that can occur when a disk is cold and massive enough for its own gravity to shape its structure. The study also reports “dust-trapping signatures”, suggesting that spiral arms may act as pressure structures where solid particles can accumulate and grow. The authors propose that material falling from the surrounding environment could trigger “infall-triggered gravitational instabilities”, making Elias 2-27 a useful example of how disk evolution, gas dynamics, and dust concentration can work together to create visible substructures [@panequecarreno2021_elias227].
:::

::: {.evolution-example-card}
::: {.example-label}
Thermal evolution
:::

### V883 Ori: when accretion moves the snowline

Disk evolution can also be strongly shaped by changes in the disk’s thermal structure. A useful example is **V883 Ori**, a FU Orionis-type object undergoing an accretion outburst. In this system, Alarcón et al. (2024) show that passive stellar irradiation alone cannot reproduce the observed millimeter continuum emission.

The authors state that “Irradiation heating by itself is not enough to explain the spiky radial continuum profile or the high-brightness temperatures in the inner regions of V883 Ori”, so an additional heat source is required.. In their model, viscous heating from accretion becomes a dominant source of energy inside the water snowline, increasing the disk temperature, changing the disk shape, and pushing condensation fronts outward. This makes V883 Ori an important reminder that snowlines are not fixed boundaries: they can move as the disk’s energy budget changes, affecting the chemistry, dust properties, and local conditions for planet formation [@alarcon2024_v883ori].
:::

:::

::: {.evolution-takeaway}
**Key idea:** disk morphology is not just appearance. Rings, gaps, spirals, arcs, crescents, and moving snowlines are observable traces of the physical processes that redistribute material, change the disk temperature, and help set the conditions for planet formation.
:::

:::

## How to use and expand this catalog {#how-to-use-catalog}

::: {.catalog-use-box}

This catalog was designed as both an **educational** and a **scientific** resource for exploring protoplanetary disks in a structured, comparative, and accessible way. Its purpose is not only to gather information about different systems, but also to help readers understand how disks are studied, what their substructures mean, and why they matter for planet formation.

Each disk page is organized to guide the reader from basic identification to scientific interpretation. In general, the pages include sections such as **object names**, **location**, **general description**, **morphology**, **dust**, **gas**, **evidence of planet formation**, and **physical interpretation**. This structure allows each system to be read both as an individual astronomical object and as part of a broader comparative context.

The catalog is also intended to be an **open, reproducible, and expandable** project. New disks, updated scientific information, new images, additional references, data science activities, and simulations can be incorporated by editing the source files in the GitHub repository. The main content is written in `.qmd` files, structured disk information is stored in `data/disks/*.json`, references are managed in `references.bib`, and the website can be rendered locally with Quarto.

For collaborators or reviewers, the repository includes a `README.md` file with instructions for opening the project, editing the catalog, adding new disks, validating the structured data, rendering the website, and contributing changes through GitHub.

[View the GitHub repository](https://github.com/martinaAbarca/pilot-protoplanetary-disks-catalog)

:::
